title: Identification of regulatory links between transcription and RNA processing with long-read sequencing
author: Alfonso-Gonzalez, Arrigoni, et al.
materials: NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module

steps.title: Preserve ultra‑long RNA fragments
steps.instruction: Wear gloves and change them frequently; use RNase‑free certified solutions and disposable plasticware with filter tips; work in a decontaminated area; add RNase inhibitors to any enzymatic reactions containing RNA; keep RNA and thawed reagents on ice until use; aliquot RNA to avoid multiple freeze‑thaw cycles; store RNA in RNase‑free water or TE buffer at –85 °C to –65 °C for up to one year; only use RNA of highest quality with no detectable fragmentation.

substeps.instruction: Wear gloves and replace them often.
Use RNase‑free solutions and filter‑tip plasticware.

Add RNase inhibitors to enzymatic reactions.
Keep RNA and reagents on ice until needed.
Aliquot RNA to prevent repeat freeze‑thaw.
Store RNA at –85 °C to –65 °C (up to 1 year).
Confirm RNA quality (no fragmentation) before proceeding.

steps.title: Prepare sequencing platform and reagents
steps.instruction: Confirm that all required reagent kits are available; ensure the Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing device is installed and fully tested; verify platform‑specific IT requirements; assign trained bioinformaticians for quality control, basecalling and downstream data analysis.

substeps.instruction: Check inventory of all reagent kits.
Install and test the ONT sequencing platform.
Review and satisfy IT specifications for the chosen platform.
Allocate bioinformatic personnel for QC, basecalling, and analysis.

steps.title: Set up R environment and install packages
steps.instruction: In R, install the devtools package, then install the LATER and LASER packages from GitHub, and load the libraries for use.

substeps.instruction: install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("hilgers-lab/LATER")
devtools::install_github("hilgers-lab/LASER")
library(LATER)
library(LASER)

steps.title: Download reference annotation
steps.instruction: Use download.file() with the appropriate URL and destination filename to retrieve the reference annotation required by LATER/LASER; repeat for each species (e.g., mouse, human) as needed.

substeps.instruction: Annotation_url <- "<URL>"  # replace with actual URL
destfile <- "<filename>"   # desired local file name
download.file(url = Annotation_url, destfile = destfile)
# Optional for mouse:
download.file(url = "<mouse_URL>", destfile = "mouse_annotation.gtf")
# Optional for human:
download.file(url = "<human_URL>", destfile = "human_annotation.gtf")

description: The protocol below describes the specific steps for sequence analysis of long RNA fragments, including instructions for both sample preparation and computational analysis. We focus our analysis on the polyadenylated fraction of the transcriptome (Poly(A)+ RNA fragments). Analysis of ultra-long RNA fragments absolutely depends on the preservation of long molecules throughout sampling and preparation steps. RNA is very susceptible to degradation by ribonucleases (RNases). Typical sources of RNase contamination are exposure to lab surfaces, aerosols from pipetting, ungloved hands or usage of contaminated reagents. Therefore, always wear gloves and exchange them frequently. Use RNase-free certified solutions and disposable plasticware, including filter tips. Use a separate, decontaminated area for RNA work and include RNase inhibitors into enzymatic reactions containing RNA fragments. Furthermore, keep RNA and thawed reagents on ice until needed and aliquot RNA samples to avoid multiple freeze-thaw cycles. Store RNA in RNase-free water or TE buffer at −85°C to −65°C for up to one year. Process only RNA of highest quality with no fragmentation detectable during initial quality assessment. This protocol relies on a number of reagent kits and equipment for sample preparation, quality controls and sequencing. Make sure all reagent kits are available and devices including a sequencing platform from Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) are installed and have been thoroughly tested. Depending on the sequencing platform in use, a high volume of data will be generated during sequencing runs. Platform-specific IT-requirements must be considered and trained bioinformaticians are needed for quality control, basecalling and data analysis.
